what.title: What is a stroke? Ischaemic and haemorrhagic stroke explained
what.description: Blocked or burst: an animated guide to ischaemic and haemorrhagic stroke, how common stroke is, lifetime risk, survival, disability and recurrence.

_homelede: A stroke happens when part of the brain loses its blood supply, or when a blood vessel in or around the brain bleeds, and brain cells are hurt or die [[Sacco2013]]. About 2 in 3 strokes come from a blocked artery and roughly 1 in 3 are bleeds; there were 11.9 million new strokes worldwide in 2021, and about 1 in 4 adults will have a stroke at some point in life [[Feigin2024,Feigin2018]]. Many people live for years afterwards: almost 94 million people are alive today after having one [[Feigin2025]].

_faq.a: A stroke happens when part of the brain loses its blood supply, or when a blood vessel in or around the brain bleeds. Brain cells then get hurt or die.

_faq.q: What are the main types of stroke?
_faq.a: There are three main types: ischaemic stroke from a blocked artery, intracerebral haemorrhage from bleeding into the brain, and subarachnoid haemorrhage from bleeding into the space around it. Worldwide in 2021 they made up about 65%, 29% and 6% of new strokes.

The Global Burden of Disease study estimated 11.9 million new strokes in 2021, and 93.8 million people living after a stroke. Stroke was the third most common cause of death in 2021, with 7.3 million deaths.

_faq.q: What is my lifetime risk of stroke?
_faq.a: Worldwide, the lifetime risk of a first stroke from age 25 was 24.9% in 2016, or about 1 in 4. It is a population figure that varies widely by region, and it cannot say what will happen to one person.

_faq.q: Can younger people have a stroke?
_faq.a: Yes. Stroke is not only a disease of old age. About 15% of new strokes worldwide happen in people aged 15 to 49, and about 53% in people under 70.

_faq.q: What is the difference between a stroke and a TIA?
_faq.a: A transient ischaemic attack (TIA) is a short episode of neurological dysfunction caused by reduced blood flow, without acute infarction. If infarction is shown and symptoms occurred, it counts as an ischaemic stroke, even when symptoms were brief. A short spell of symptoms that goes away can still be a warning sign.

_faq.q: What raises the risk of stroke most?
_faq.a: High systolic blood pressure is the largest single attributable risk, linked to 56.8% of stroke DALYs (years of healthy life lost). Worldwide, 84.1% of stroke DALYs in 2021 were attributed to the 23 risk factors analysed.

_faq.q: Can a person have a second stroke?
_faq.a: Yes. Pooled across 13 studies, about 11.1% of people had another stroke within 1 year, 26.4% within 5 years and 39.2% within 10 years. Figures vary between studies and describe groups, not individuals.
